title: Others know futures in the decree alone: Scotus and others, Calvin, and Twisse against Penot and Suárez
source_text: XXXIII. At vero sunt alii in Schola Romana Doctores, qui praesentiam istam futurorum in aeternitate, secundum proprias suas existentias, rejicientes ut vanam atque commentitiam, affirmant omnia futura contingentia, tam quae ex causis secundis liberis, quam quae ex aliis causis naturalibus eveniunt, in solo divino decreto, quo illa fieri decrevit, certo & infallibiliter cognosci. Quae opinio multis veteribus Scholasticis tribui solet, Veluti Scoto, Ricardo, Herveo, & Joanni Majori, aliisque non paucis. Atque hanc quoque sententiam amplectuntur Theologi inter Reformatos plurimi, docentes cum Calvino, Deum non alia ratione praevidere quae futura sunt, quam quia ut fierent decrevit: Praesertim vero Gulielmus Tuissus inter Theologos Anglos celeberrimus, istam Calvini Doctrinam pluribus explicat, tuetur & illustrat, tota fere dissertatione de scientia Media, adversus Penotrum & Suaresium.
pass_a_gloss: XXXIII. But indeed there are others in the Roman School Doctors, who rejecting that presence of futures in eternity, according to their own proper existences, as vain and fictitious, affirm that all future contingents, as well those which come to pass from free second causes, as those which come to pass from other natural causes, are certainly and infallibly known in the sole divine decree, by which he decreed them to be done. Which opinion is wont to be attributed to many old Scholastics, As to Scotus, Richard, Hervaeus, and John Major, and not a few others. And this opinion too very many Theologians among the Reformed embrace, teaching with Calvin, that God foresees what things are future by no other reason, than because he decreed that they should be done: But especially William Twisse most celebrated among the English Theologians, explains, defends and illustrates at length that Doctrine of Calvin, in almost the whole dissertation on Middle knowledge, against Penot and Suárez.
pass_b_english: There are, however, other teachers in the Roman school who reject this presence of future things in eternity in their own existences as empty and invented. They hold that every future contingent, whether it comes from free second causes or from other natural causes, is known with certainty and without fail in God's decree alone, by which he decreed that it should happen. This view is usually attributed to many of the older scholastics, such as Scotus, Richard, Hervaeus, John Major and a good number of others.

Very many Reformed theologians also embrace it, teaching with Calvin that God foresees what will happen for no other reason than that he decreed it should happen. William Twisse, among the most celebrated English theologians, sets out, defends and illustrates this teaching of Calvin at length, through almost the whole of his dissertation on middle knowledge, written against Penot and Suárez.

choices.why: God's decree; 'decree' is kept throughout, with 'decreed' for decrevit.
